meta.title: Answer Sense
meta.intro: Every question here comes with a common answer that is scientifically true and still does not score. The point is not the science, which you may already know. The point is the gap between a true statement and an answer that responds to what was asked. Read the question, decide in your head what the answer must contain, then reveal the common answer and the thinking behind why it falls short.

failureTypes.label: Named a keyword, not the mechanism
failureTypes.blurb: The right process is named, but the answer stops there. It is too short: it never says where things came from or what drove the change.

failureTypes.label: Gave the evidence, not the conclusion
failureTypes.blurb: The observation is restated as if it were the answer. An infer or conclude question wants the step from evidence to conclusion.

failureTypes.label: Answered half the question
failureTypes.blurb: A two-part question, or one with a comparison clause, was answered on one side only. Half the marks were left on the table.

failureTypes.label: True but too general
failureTypes.blurb: The statement is correct but generic. It was never tied to this scenario, this animal, this habitat, so it could have been written without reading the question.

failureTypes.label: Restated the question
failureTypes.blurb: The prediction or observation was repeated back with no reason attached. The marks were for the reason, not the restatement.

failureTypes.label: Compared one-sidedly
failureTypes.blurb: A property of one thing was given instead of a contrast between both. A compare answer must set the two against each other.

items.stimulus: Ahmad takes an ice-cold can of drink out of the fridge on a hot day. After a few minutes, water droplets form on the outside of the can.
items.stem: Explain how these water droplets formed.
items.whatItLooksLike: Name the process that made the droplets appear.
items.whatItsAsking: Trace the whole formation: where the water came from, what made it happen, and the result.
items.hiddenTest: Whether the student can build a change-of-state mechanism, and whether they avoid the misconception that the water came from inside the can.
items.weakAnswer: The water vapour turned into water droplets.
items.thinkingGap: He treated an explain-how-it-formed question as name-the-process, and stopped the moment he recognised condensation. A formation question has three hidden parts: where the water came from (water vapour in the surrounding air, not from inside the can), what drove it (the cold surface of the can, so the vapour lost heat), and the result (it condensed into droplets). He wrote only the third. An answer that names the change but not its source or cause is a keyword, not an explanation.
items.strongAnswer: There is water vapour in the surrounding air. When it comes into contact with the cold surface of the can, it loses heat and condenses into water droplets on the outside of the can.
items.whyItWorks: Two marks, two demands: it names the source (water vapour in the air) and the driver (contact with the cold surface, losing heat) before naming the result, so the mechanism is complete.
items.attentionCue: Explain how it formed = it came FROM somewhere + something MADE it happen + the result.

items.stimulus: Priya places different materials, one at a time, into the gap in a circuit. For some materials the bulb lights up; for others it does not.
items.stem: Infer which materials are conductors of electricity and which are insulators, and explain how you decided.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what happened to the bulb.
items.whatItsAsking: Draw the conclusion (which is which) and give the reasoning that links the bulb to that conclusion.
items.hiddenTest: Whether the student can move from an observation to a justified conclusion, rather than repeating the observation the question already supplied.
items.weakAnswer: The bulb lit up for the metal materials.
items.thinkingGap: An infer question wants a conclusion and the reasoning behind it, never the observation. The bulb lighting is the evidence the examiner already handed him in the stimulus, so repeating it earns nothing. The marks live in the step he skipped: bulb lights, so electricity flows through the material, so it is a conductor. If a sentence could have been written just by looking at the picture, no inference has happened yet.
items.strongAnswer: The materials for which the bulb lit up are conductors; the materials for which the bulb did not light are insulators. When the bulb lights up, it shows that electricity is able to flow through the material, so it is a conductor. When the bulb does not light up, no electricity flows through the material, so it is an insulator.
items.whyItWorks: Three marks: the conclusion labels both groups, and each label is justified by the reasoning that ties the bulb to whether current flows. The observation is used as evidence, not offered as the answer.
items.attentionCue: If your sentence could have been written just by looking at the picture, you have not inferred yet.
